read_from: The route text as served: field 1 (the route text) of each row of reader/data/route-store of the main branch at commit 306f3b285898, store_version 87b13b1169b4 (its index.json), for "UBS Dictionary of Biblical Hebrew v0.9.2 exact definitions and glosses" (M18): 21,626 routes (axis: routes), 6,539 letters keys (axis: keys). The definition field of the same row equals the route text on 21,626 of the routes and was read only to understand a route. The source audit compares each route with the lane's copy of the source (the store record of M18, the dictionary's own JSON) after the store's own stripping: 17,344 routes come from a sense's short definition field, 4,265 from its gloss list, 2 from both, and 15 match neither by exact comparison (axis: routes); the audit is evidence about the source and no part of any test. The source's own key to its signs: the README of the dictionary (ubsicap/ubs-open-license at commit 3a6edd82, dictionaries/hebrew) explains its tags for a footnote, a link, a Scripture reference and a cited work, which the store strips, and lists the abbreviations of cited works; it gives no account of =, ◄, ►, ≈, >, the code |i and |i*, or the letters in [a] and [b], so every shape whose meaning says what one of those signs is for begins "unverified:".

definitions.first_match: For each mark the shapes are tried in the order of this declaration; the first shape whose test holds names the occurrence, and no later shape is tried for it. Not caught above means that no earlier shape of the same mark took the occurrence. A shape's container field is not part of its test: a test looks at the container only where its words say so, and the checker compares the field afterwards.
definitions.character_words: Whitespace is any character that JavaScript's regular-expression class backslash-s matches. A letter is any character with the Unicode property Letter, in any script. A number character is any character with the Unicode property Number. A digit is one of 0 to 9. A word character is a letter, a number character or an underscore. A Hebrew letter is a character from U+05D0 to U+05EA. A character is one Unicode code point; no route holds a character beyond 16 bits, so a 16-bit unit gives the same results. The double quotation mark is U+0022 only, not a curly mark. In the tests and in these definitions a string stands between « and », which are not part of it. Every string written in a test or a definition and every string of a list matches case-sensitively and exactly as written, unless the words say case not minded; then both sides are compared in lowercase, as JavaScript's toLowerCase gives them. The text before the mark and the text after the mark are the route text on either side of the mark, the mark itself in neither, and neither is trimmed unless the words say so. Once trimmed means with the whitespace taken off both ends. Contains means that the string stands anywhere in the text as a run of characters, with or without a word boundary beside it, also where the words say contains one of the words of a list. Begins with and ends with compare characters in the same way, unless a step adds a boundary.
definitions.unbalanced: Scan the characters of the whole route text from left to right with a stack. An opening ( [ < or { is pushed. A closing ) ] > or } pops the stack when the top of the stack is its own opening bracket (( for ), [ for ], < for >, { for }); when the stack is empty or its top is another opener, the text is unbalanced at once. At the end the text is also unbalanced when the stack is not empty.
definitions.next_is: Take the text after the mark and remove the whitespace at its start. The step holds for a list when at least one listed string passes both of these: that text begins with the string, and the character right after the string, if there is one, is not a word character (character_words). Every listed string is tried, so where two listed strings both begin the text, the step holds if either passes.
definitions.prev_is: Take the text before the mark and remove the whitespace at its end. The step holds for a list when at least one listed string passes both of these: that text ends with the string, and the character right before the string, if there is one, is not a word character (character_words). Every listed string is tried, so where two listed strings both end the text, the step holds if either passes.
definitions.next_char: The first character of the text after the mark once the whitespace at its start is removed; nothing if that leaves no text.
definitions.prev_char: The last character of the text before the mark once the whitespace at its end is removed; nothing if that leaves no text.
definitions.opens_with_opener: The route text, from its very first character, begins with one of the words in opener_words, and the character right after that word, if there is one, is not a word character (character_words).
definitions.opens_with_label: The route text, from its very first character, begins with one of the strings in head_labels, and the character right after that string, if there is one, is not a word character (character_words).
definitions.opens_with_literal_name: The route opens_with_opener. Take the route text, take off that opener word, then take off every character that follows it as long as the character is whitespace, a colon, a comma or the double quotation mark. The step holds when what remains begins, case not minded, with one of the strings in literal_names. No boundary is looked at after the string.
definitions.piece_opens_with_title: Take the text after the mark. Take off from its start, in this order and each only if it stands there: whitespace; the word «hence» or the word «therefore» (the character right after the word not being a word character); whitespace; the word «also» (the same); whitespace; one comma, colon or semicolon; whitespace; the word «possibly» or the word «probably» (the same); whitespace; one comma, colon or semicolon; whitespace; one equals sign; whitespace. Then, case not minded, take off «a», «an» or «the» with the whitespace after it, if it stands there followed by whitespace. The step holds when what remains begins, case not minded, with one of the words in title_words and the character right after the word, if there is one, is not a word character.
definitions.wording_speaks_of_the_turn: Look at the text before the mark. The step holds when either of these holds: (1) for some comma in that text, the part of that text after the comma, its whitespace removed at the start, begins with one of the strings in turn_words_after_comma, and the character right after the string, if there is one, is not a word character; (2) that text contains one of the strings in turn_phrases.
definitions.wording_and_meaning_semicolon: For a semicolon. If the route opens_with_opener, the step holds when any one of these holds: (1) the text after the semicolon passes next_is with «hence» and «therefore»; (2) the next_char of the text after the semicolon is «=»; (3) the text before the semicolon contains no semicolon, and the text after it passes next_is with «exact», «possibly», «probably» and «figuratively». If the route does not open that way, the step holds when both of these hold: the text before the semicolon contains no semicolon; and the text after it passes next_is with the one word «hence».
definitions.wording_and_meaning_colon: For a colon. The step holds when all of these hold: the route opens_with_opener; the text before the colon contains no semicolon; and the text after the colon either has the next_char «=» or passes next_is with the one word «hence».
definitions.shared_note: Find every semicolon of the route text whose text after it passes next_is with alternative_openers. The first alternative is the route text before the first of these semicolons; the last alternative is the route text after the last of them. The route has a shared note when either of these holds: (1) the last alternative contains «►» and the first alternative does not; (2) the last alternative contains «◄», «►» or «≈» and the first alternative contains none of the three.
definitions.note_only_after_the_mark: The text after the mark contains «◄», «►» or «≈», and the text before the mark contains none of the three.
definitions.round_bracket_kind: What a round bracket holds is the text between it and its partner, as the template gives it (c.group). Its words are that text split at runs of whitespace, empty pieces dropped, with one comma taken off the end of a word that ends in a comma. Its kind is the first of these that fits, in this order. nothing: once trimmed it is empty. ending: it is exactly «s». prefix: it is exactly «semi-» or exactly «-point». item: it is exactly one digit, or exactly one of «a», «b», «c». citation: its first word is one of citation_words. date: it begins with a digit, or its first word is exactly «c.» or exactly «ca.». pointer: its first word is exactly «see». slot: its first word is one of slot_words, or its first word is one of slot_prepositions and its second word is one of slot_words. other: anything else.

homonyms.reason: The route text carries no entry number. The source's own file gives every entry an id (MainId), every sense an id (LEXID) and its Strong's codes, all of which the store dropped; two entries under one letters key stand there as separate texts with nothing to tell them apart (example key דמע: its 2 route texts come from the source's entries 001684000000000 and 001685000000000). keys_with_more_than_one_route_text counts senses and homonyms together. By the audit, of the 3,136 such keys (axis: keys; 6,539 letters keys in all) 1,991 are keys for which one single entry of the source yields every distinct route text, and 1,145 are keys for which no single entry does, so that the texts come from two or more entries that share the letters, true homonyms.

branches.question: The source often gives the Hebrew word for word and then what that wording means, inside one text, like: literally: to dig (an area); hence: = action by which ... Should the word-for-word wording and what it means be two readings? A proper name or a title with its description, a wording that itself says how it turns to the meaning or that holds a description, a short gloss written with the sign >, and a text whose brackets do not pair stay as one reading under either answer. A text that opens with a label, or whose wording says in what kind of text it is found, has its own question, B04.

options.means: The page prints the wording as one reading and what it means as another, with any lead word of the source's own and the notes that follow it: literally: to dig (an area), and hence: = action by which ... Where a text takes two such steps, each step is its own reading.
The page keeps the wording and what it means together in one reading, as the source writes it.

branches.question: Inside one entry of its gloss list the source sometimes writes two words side by side, each of which could render the Hebrew alone, like: pain, trouble. Should they be two readings? The ledger holds these texts in a written list, so nothing here is a guess about the kind of text, and the same question covers two interjections written side by side in one gloss. Glosses whose words lean on each other are not in the list and stay as one reading.

options.means: The page prints two readings, the words on each side of the mark: pain, and trouble.
The page prints the gloss as one reading, as the source writes it: pain, trouble.

branches.question: In a few texts the source offers two or more meanings side by side, parted by a comma, a semicolon or a full stop, like: a fortified town, or a fortified place within a town. Should each meaning be its own reading? The ledger lists these texts by hand, because no test can find them, so they wait for you. A text that opens with a label saying how sure the source is or what kind of word this is, or that has a note only after the last part, has its own question, B04. Today the page cuts at each semicolon outside round brackets and then by its comma rule, and prints a fortified town beside the whole text. From the day this is wired it prints what you answer, and one reading until you answer.

options.means: The page prints each meaning as its own reading, with the source's own lead word: a fortified town, and or a fortified place within a town or on its walls. Nothing moves: words at the head that cover both stay with the first piece, and words after the last meaning that cover both stay with the last piece.
The page keeps the meanings together in one reading, as the source writes them.

branches.question: Some texts hold two or more parts under one label or one note: a label in the first part says how sure the source is, what kind of word this is or in what kind of text it is found, or a note stands only after the last part, and that label or note can speak of every part, like: meaning unknown; possibly: = musical term; or: = musical ... Should the parts print as separate readings? A text whose second part leans on the first, or whose first part holds no wording of its own, stays as one reading under either answer.

options.means: The page prints each part as its own reading, with the source's own lead word. Nothing moves: the label stays with the first piece and a closing note stays with the last.
The page keeps the parts together in one reading, as the source writes them.

not_done_here: This ledger leaves every ◄, ► and ≈ note in the piece it follows, because the ask counts a note as no reading and gives it no piece of its own; it leaves a pointer at the end of a text (see ...) in the last piece; and it leaves to the store what the store does to the source's text: it takes off the source's tags and the sign = at the start of a definition, closes a space before a mark, takes the invisible U+200E off, and reads a tag written with escaped brackets.
